import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Line graphs of word-representable graphs

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [Wikipedia, Line graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/line_graph)
- [Wikipedia, Word-representable graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word-representable_graph)
-/

namespace LineGraph

/-- Two letters alternate in a word if, after all other letters are deleted, no two consecutive
letters are equal. -/
def Alternates {V : Type*} (w : List V) (x y : V) : Prop := by
  classical
  exact (w.filter fun z => z = x ∨ z = y).IsChain (· ≠ ·)

/-- A graph is word-representable if there is a finite word containing every vertex in which two
distinct letters alternate exactly when the corresponding vertices are adjacent. -/
def WordRepresentable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, (∀ x, x ∈ w) ∧
    ∀ x y, x ≠ y → (Alternates w x y ↔ G.Adj x y)

/--
Is the line graph of a non-word-representable finite simple graph always
non-word-representable? Equivalently, does every finite simple graph `G` satisfy
`¬ WordRepresentable G → ¬ WordRepresentable G.lineGraph`?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem line_graph :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (V : Type) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V),
      ¬ WordRepresentable G → ¬ WordRepresentable G.lineGraph := by
  sorry

end LineGraph
modeling_decisions: Interpreted the yes/no question positively: `answer(True)` says that every finite simple non-word-representable graph has a non-word-representable line graph.

Modeled finite simple graphs as `SimpleGraph V` with `[Fintype V]`, including empty and edgeless graphs; no nonemptiness restriction is imposed because these graphs are word-representable under the standard definition.
Modeled a word as `List V` and required every vertex to occur at least once.

For distinct vertices `x` and `y`, modeled alternation by filtering the word to those two letters and requiring every consecutive pair in the filtered list to be unequal. The distinctness condition is essential because word-representability tests unordered pairs of distinct vertices.
Used Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.lineGraph`, whose vertices are edges of the original graph and whose adjacency relation is incidence of distinct edges.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Line graphs of non-word-representable graphs

A graph $G = (V, E)$ is *word-representable* if there is a word $w$ over the alphabet $V$,
containing every letter of $V$, such that two distinct letters $x, y$ alternate in $w$
if and only if $xy \in E$. Here $x$ and $y$ *alternate* in $w$ if deleting from $w$ all
letters other than $x$ and $y$ leaves a word of the form $xyxy\cdots$ or $yxyx\cdots$.

The *line graph* $L(G)$ of $G$ has the edges of $G$ as vertices, two of them being adjacent
when the corresponding edges of $G$ share an endpoint (Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.lineGraph`).

Kitaev, Salimov, Severs and Úlfarsson showed that iterating the line graph operation
eventually produces non-word-representable graphs (for any connected graph other than a path,
a cycle or the claw $K_{1,3}$). It is an open question whether the line graph of a
non-word-representable graph is always non-word-representable.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Line graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/line_graph)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics#Graph_theory)
- [Wikipedia, Word-representable graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word-representable_graph)
- S. Kitaev, V. Lozin, *Words and Graphs*, Monographs in Theoretical Computer Science,
  Springer, 2015.
- [S. Kitaev, *A comprehensive introduction to the theory of word-representable graphs*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.05924)
- S. Kitaev, P. Salimov, C. Severs, H. Úlfarsson, *On the representability of line graphs*,
  WORDS 2011, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 6795 (2011), 478–479.
-/

namespace LineGraph

variable {V : Type*}

open scoped Classical in
/--
Two letters `x` and `y` *alternate* in the word `w` if, after deleting from `w` all letters
other than `x` and `y`, no two consecutive letters of the resulting word are equal. When both
`x` and `y` occur in `w`, this says that the resulting word is of the form `xyxy…` or `yxyx…`.
-/
def Alternate (w : List V) (x y : V) : Prop :=
  (w.filter fun z => z = x ∨ z = y).IsChain (· ≠ ·)

/--
A word `w` over the alphabet `V` *represents* the graph `G` on `V` if every vertex occurs in `w`
and two distinct vertices alternate in `w` if and only if they are adjacent in `G`.
-/
def Represents (w : List V) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  (∀ v, v ∈ w) ∧ ∀ x y, x ≠ y → (Alternate w x y ↔ G.Adj x y)

/-- A graph is *word-representable* if some word over its vertex set represents it. -/
def WordRepresentable (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, Represents w G

@[category API, AMS 5 68]
theorem alternate_comm (w : List V) (x y : V) : Alternate w x y ↔ Alternate w y x := by
  simp only [Alternate]
  rw [List.filter_congr fun z _ => decide_eq_decide.mpr or_comm]

/-- The word `xy` represents the complete graph on two vertices. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem wordRepresentable_top_fin_two : WordRepresentable (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)) := by
  refine ⟨[0, 1], by decide, fun x y hxy => ?_⟩
  fin_cases x <;> fin_cases y <;> simp_all [Alternate]

/-- The word `xxyy` represents the edgeless graph on two vertices. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem wordRepresentable_bot_fin_two : WordRepresentable (⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)) := by
  refine ⟨[0, 0, 1, 1], by decide, fun x y hxy => ?_⟩
  fin_cases x <;> fin_cases y <;> simp_all [Alternate]

/-- The empty word represents the graph with no vertices. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem wordRepresentable_of_isEmpty [IsEmpty V] (G : SimpleGraph V) : WordRepresentable G :=
  ⟨[], fun v => isEmptyElim v, fun x => isEmptyElim x⟩

/--
Is the line graph of a non-word-representable graph always non-word-representable?

That is, is it true that for every finite simple graph $G$, if $G$ is not word-representable,
then its line graph $L(G)$ is not word-representable either?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 68]
theorem line_graph :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∀ {V : Type*} [Finite V] (G : SimpleGraph V),
        ¬ WordRepresentable G → ¬ WordRepresentable G.lineGraph := by
  sorry

end LineGraph
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The table's single-slot reading (a yes/no question with `answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ finite simple G, ¬WR G → ¬WR L(G)`) matches the source and is what the file states.
modeling_decisions: Graphs are required to be finite via `[Finite V]`. This is implicit in the source (all of Kitaev's theory concerns finite graphs) and is essential: no graph on an infinite vertex type is word-representable (a finite word cannot contain every letter), so without finiteness an infinite graph with a single edge would have a one-vertex, word-representable line graph and the statement would be trivially false.

Word-representability follows the Kitaev–Lozin definition: a word over the vertex alphabet in which every vertex occurs, such that distinct letters x, y alternate iff xy is an edge. Alternation is formalized as: the subword of occurrences of x and y has no two equal consecutive letters (`List.IsChain (· ≠ ·)`), which for letters that both occur is exactly 'of the form xyxy… or yxyx…'.

The line graph is Mathlib's `SimpleGraph.lineGraph`, whose vertex type is `G.edgeSet` (two edges adjacent iff distinct and sharing an endpoint); this matches the standard line graph of a simple graph. No decidability instances are needed since word-representability is defined via existence of a list.
The vertex type is quantified universe-polymorphically (`∀ {V : Type*}`), following existing repo files such as SidorenkoConjecture.lean and ErdosProblems/184.lean.

`answer(True)` means 'yes: the line graph of every finite non-word-representable graph is non-word-representable'; `answer(False)` means some finite non-word-representable graph has a word-representable line graph. The hypothesis is satisfiable (e.g. the wheel W₅ is non-word-representable), and edgeless/empty graphs are word-representable, so degenerate cases never trigger the implication.

The Wikipedia line-graph article contains no material on word-representability; the precise formulation is taken from Kitaev–Lozin 'Words and Graphs', Kitaev's survey arXiv:1705.05924, and Kitaev–Salimov–Severs–Úlfarsson 'On the representability of line graphs', all cited in the module docstring together with the required Wikipedia URL.

The `open scoped Classical in` is scoped to the single definition `Alternate` (per AGENTS.md); API/test statements (`alternate_comm`, representability of K₂, of the edgeless 2-vertex graph, and of the empty graph) are included with short proofs as required for bespoke definitions.

Word-representability is not in Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib, so it is defined in the file following Kitaev–Lozin: a word (List V) containing every vertex such that two distinct vertices alternate in the word iff they are adjacent.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Line graphs of non-word-representable graphs

Two distinct letters $x$ and $y$ *alternate* in a word $w$ if, after deleting from $w$ all
letters other than $x$ and $y$, one obtains a word of the form $xyxy\dots$ or $yxyx\dots$
(of even or odd length).

A finite simple graph $G = (V, E)$ is *word-representable* if there is a word $w$ over the
alphabet $V$, in which every letter of $V$ occurs at least once, such that two distinct letters
$x, y \in V$ alternate in $w$ if and only if $xy \in E$.

The *line graph* $L(G)$ of $G$ has the edges of $G$ as vertices, two of them being adjacent when
the corresponding edges of $G$ share an endpoint.

Kitaev, Salimov, Severs and Úlfarsson showed that many line graphs are not word-representable
(for instance $L(K_n)$ for $n \ge 5$, and $L^k(G)$ for $k \ge 4$ whenever $G$ is connected and
is neither a path, nor a cycle, nor the claw $K_{1,3}$). The following question is open:
is the line graph of a non-word-representable graph always non-word-representable?

*References:*
- [Wikipedia: Line graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/line_graph)
- [Wikipedia: Word-representable graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word-representable_graph)
- [Wikipedia: List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- S. Kitaev, *A comprehensive introduction to the theory of word-representable graphs*,
  [arXiv:1705.05924](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.05924).
- S. Kitaev, P. Salimov, C. Severs, H. Úlfarsson, *On the representability of line graphs*,
  Developments in Language Theory (DLT 2011), LNCS 6795, 478--479.
- S. Kitaev, V. Lozin, *Words and Graphs*, Springer, 2015.
-/

namespace LineGraph

open SimpleGraph

open scoped Classical in
/-- Two letters `x` and `y` *alternate* in the word `w` if, after deleting from `w` all letters
other than `x` and `y`, no two consecutive letters of the resulting word are equal, i.e. the
resulting word is of the form `xyxy…` or `yxyx…`. -/
def Alternate {V : Type*} (w : List V) (x y : V) : Prop :=
  (w.filter fun z => z = x ∨ z = y).IsChain (· ≠ ·)

/-- A simple graph `G` on the vertex type `V` is *word-representable* if there is a (finite) word
`w` over the alphabet `V`, in which every vertex occurs at least once, such that two distinct
vertices `x` and `y` alternate in `w` if and only if they are adjacent in `G`. -/
def WordRepresentable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, (∀ v, v ∈ w) ∧ ∀ x y, x ≠ y → (G.Adj x y ↔ Alternate w x y)

/-- Alternation of two letters in a word is a symmetric relation. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 68]
theorem alternate_comm {V : Type*} (w : List V) (x y : V) :
    Alternate w x y ↔ Alternate w y x := by
  unfold Alternate
  rw [List.filter_congr fun z _ => decide_eq_decide.mpr or_comm]

/-- A word-representable graph has only finitely many vertices, since its word-representant is a
finite word containing every vertex. -/
@[category API, AMS 5 68]
theorem WordRepresentable.finite {V : Type*} {G : SimpleGraph V} (hG : WordRepresentable G) :
    Finite V := by
  obtain ⟨w, hw, -⟩ := hG
  exact Finite.of_surjective (fun i : Fin w.length => w.get i) fun v => List.mem_iff_get.mp (hw v)

/-- The complete graph on three vertices is word-representable, via the word `012`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem wordRepresentable_top_fin_three : WordRepresentable (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) := by
  refine ⟨[0, 1, 2], by decide, ?_⟩
  simp [Alternate, Fin.forall_fin_succ, List.filter_cons]

/-- The edgeless graph on two vertices is word-representable, via the word `0110`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5 68]
theorem wordRepresentable_bot_fin_two : WordRepresentable (⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin 2)) := by
  refine ⟨[0, 1, 1, 0], by decide, ?_⟩
  simp [Alternate, Fin.forall_fin_succ, List.filter_cons]

/--
Is the line graph of a non-word-representable graph always non-word-representable?

That is, is it true that for every finite simple graph $G$, if $G$ is not word-representable,
then its line graph $L(G)$ is not word-representable either?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 68]
theorem line_graph :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V),
      ¬ WordRepresentable G → ¬ WordRepresentable G.lineGraph := by
  sorry

end LineGraph
attempts.decomposition_objections: None. The table's reading (single yes/no question, finite simple graphs, word-representability defined via alternation with every vertex occurring) matches the source and Kitaev's standard definitions; the file conforms to it.
modeling_decisions: Graphs are taken finite (`[Fintype V]`) and simple (`SimpleGraph`), as implicit in the source. Finiteness is necessary, not just cosmetic: an infinite edgeless graph is never word-representable by a finite word, yet its line graph is the empty graph, which is word-representable; without `[Fintype V]` the question would trivially have a negative answer for a spurious reason.

Word-representability requires every vertex to occur at least once in the word, following Kitaev's definition ('by definition, w must contain each letter in V'). Consequently the empty graph on an empty vertex type is word-representable (empty word), and word-representability implies finiteness of V (recorded as the API lemma `WordRepresentable.finite`).

Alternation is formalized as: the filtered subword on {x,y} has no two equal consecutive letters (`List.IsChain (· ≠ ·)`). For distinct x, y both present in the word this is exactly the 'xyxy… or yxyx…' condition. `WordRepresentable` only evaluates `Alternate` at x ≠ y.

`Alternate` uses `open scoped Classical in` for the `List.filter` predicate rather than a `[DecidableEq V]` hypothesis, so the main statement carries no decidability instances; tests are proved by `simp` instead of `decide`.

Answer polarity: `answer(True)` means 'yes, the line graph of a non-word-representable finite graph is always non-word-representable'; `answer(False)` means a finite non-word-representable graph with word-representable line graph exists.
Vertex type quantified as `∀ {V : Type*} [Fintype V]` inside the iff (as in the repo's `CernyConjecture.lean`) rather than restricting to `Fin n`; this is equivalent up to isomorphism.
AMS tags 5 (combinatorics) and 68 (computer science; combinatorics on words, 68R15).

alphabet $V$, in which every letter of $V$ occurs, such that two distinct letters $x, y$
alternate in $w$ if and only if $xy \in E$. Here $x$ and $y$ *alternate* in $w$ if deleting all
other letters from $w$ leaves a word of the form $xyxy\cdots$ or $yxyx\cdots$.

The problem asks whether the line graph of a non-word-representable graph is always
non-word-representable.

*References:*
* [Wikipedia, Line graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/line_graph)
* [Wikipedia, Word-representable graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Word-representable_graph)
* [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
* [KSSU11] Kitaev, S., Salimov, P., Severs, C., Úlfarsson, H. (2011). "On the representability
  of line graphs." *Combinatorics on Words, WORDS 2011*, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 6795,
  pp. 478--479.
* [KL15] Kitaev, S., Lozin, V. (2015). *Words and Graphs*. Springer.
-/

namespace LineGraph

open SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*}

open scoped Classical in
/-- Two letters `x` and `y` *alternate* in a word `w` if, after deleting from `w` all letters other
than `x` and `y`, no two consecutive letters of the remaining word are equal, i.e. the remaining
word is of the form `xyxy…` or `yxyx…`. -/
def Alternate (w : List V) (x y : V) : Prop :=
  (w.filter fun z => z = x ∨ z = y).IsChain (· ≠ ·)

/-- A word `w` over the alphabet `V` *represents* the graph `G` on `V` if every vertex of `G`
occurs in `w` and two distinct vertices `x` and `y` are adjacent in `G` if and only if `x` and
`y` alternate in `w`. -/
def Represents (w : List V) (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  (∀ v, v ∈ w) ∧ ∀ x y, x ≠ y → (G.Adj x y ↔ Alternate w x y)

/-- A graph `G` is *word-representable* if some word over its vertex set represents it. -/
def WordRepresentable (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, Represents w G

/-- A graph with infinitely many vertices is never word-representable, since a word is finite.
This is why the conjecture below is restricted to finite graphs. -/
@[category API, AMS 5]
theorem not_wordRepresentable_of_infinite [Infinite V] (G : SimpleGraph V) :
    ¬ WordRepresentable G := by
  rintro ⟨w, hw, -⟩
  exact (Set.infinite_univ.mono fun v _ => hw v) w.finite_toSet

/-- The complete graph $K_3$ is represented by the word $012$. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem wordRepresentable_top_fin_three : WordRepresentable (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) := by
  refine ⟨[0, 1, 2], fun v => ?_, fun x y hxy => ?_⟩
  · fin_cases v <;> simp
  · fin_cases x <;> fin_cases y <;> simp_all [Alternate, List.filter]

/-- The path $P_3$ on the vertices $0, 1, 2$ (with edges $01$ and $12$) is represented by the word
$01021$. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem wordRepresentable_pathGraph_three : WordRepresentable (pathGraph 3) := by
  refine ⟨[0, 1, 0, 2, 1], fun v => ?_, fun x y hxy => ?_⟩
  · fin_cases v <;> simp
  · fin_cases x <;> fin_cases y <;> simp_all [Alternate, List.filter, pathGraph_adj]

/--
Is the line graph of a non-word-representable graph always non-word-representable?

That is, is it true that for every finite simple graph $G$, if $G$ is not word-representable then
its line graph $L(G)$ is not word-representable either?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5 68]
theorem line_graph : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∀ {V : Type*} [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V),
      ¬ WordRepresentable G → ¬ WordRepresentable G.lineGraph := by
  sorry

end LineGraph

namespace LineGraph

/--
A simple graph is word-representable if there is a word over its vertex set which contains every

Is the line graph of every finite simple non-word-representable graph also
non-word-representable?

A (finite, simple) graph $G = (V, E)$ is *word-representable* if there is a word $w$ over the
alphabet $V$, containing every letter of $V$ at least once, such that two distinct letters
$x, y$ alternate in $w$ if and only if $xy \in E$. Two letters $x$ and $y$ *alternate* in $w$ if
deleting from $w$ all letters other than $x$ and $y$ leaves a word of the form $xyxy\cdots$ or

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Line graph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/line_graph)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in
  mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)

- S. Kitaev, P. Salimov, C. Severs, H. Úlfarsson, *Word-representability of line graphs*,
  Open Journal of Discrete Mathematics 1 (2011), 96–101.
- S. Kitaev, V. Lozin, *Words and Graphs*, Springer (2015).
- [S. Kitaev, *A comprehensive introduction to the theory of word-representable graphs*,
  arXiv:1705.05924](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.05924)
-/

namespace LineGraph

open SimpleGraph

variable {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V]

/--
Two letters `x` and `y` *alternate* in the word `w` if, after deleting from `w` all letters other
than `x` and `y`, no two consecutive letters of the remaining word are equal, i.e. the remaining
word is of the form `xyxy…` or `yxyx…` (of even or odd length).
-/
def Alternate (w : List V) (x y : V) : Prop :=
  (w.filter fun z => z = x ∨ z = y).IsChain (· ≠ ·)

/--
A word `w` over the alphabet `V` *represents* the graph `G` if every vertex of `G` occurs in `w`
and two distinct vertices `x` and `y` alternate in `w` if and only if `xy` is an edge of `G`.
-/
def Represents (G : SimpleGraph V) (w : List V) : Prop :=
  (∀ v, v ∈ w) ∧ ∀ x y, x ≠ y → (Alternate w x y ↔ G.Adj x y)

/-- A graph is *word-representable* if some word over its vertex set represents it. -/
def WordRepresentable (G : SimpleGraph V) : Prop :=
  ∃ w : List V, Represents G w

/-- The letters `0` and `1` alternate in the word `0 1 0`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem alternate_example : Alternate ([0, 1, 0] : List (Fin 2)) 0 1 := by
  unfold Alternate
  decide

/-- The letters `0` and `1` do not alternate in the word `0 0 1`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem not_alternate_example : ¬ Alternate ([0, 0, 1] : List (Fin 2)) 0 1 := by
  unfold Alternate
  decide

/-- The complete graph on three vertices is represented by the word `0 1 2`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem wordRepresentable_top_fin_three : WordRepresentable (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) :=
  ⟨[0, 1, 2], by unfold Represents Alternate; decide⟩

/-- The edgeless graph on three vertices is represented by the word `0 0 1 1 2 2`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem wordRepresentable_bot_fin_three : WordRepresentable (⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)) :=
  ⟨[0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2], by unfold Represents Alternate; decide⟩

/-- The path `0 — 1 — 2` on three vertices is represented by the word `1 0 2 1 2 0`. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem wordRepresentable_path_fin_three :
    WordRepresentable (fromRel fun a b : Fin 3 => a.val + 1 = b.val) :=
  ⟨[1, 0, 2, 1, 2, 0], by unfold Represents Alternate; decide⟩

/-- The line graph of the edgeless graph on three vertices is word-representable. -/
@[category test, AMS 5]
theorem wordRepresentable_lineGraph_bot_fin_three :
    WordRepresentable (⊥ : SimpleGraph (Fin 3)).lineGraph :=
  ⟨[], fun e => (by simpa using e.2 : False).elim,
    fun e _ _ => (by simpa using e.2 : False).elim⟩

/--
Is the line graph of a non-word-representable graph always non-word-representable?

That is, for every finite simple graph $G$: if $G$ is not word-representable, then its line
graph $L(G)$ (whose vertices are the edges of $G$, two of them adjacent when they share an
endpoint) is not word-representable either.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 5]
theorem line_graph :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (V : Type*) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V),
      ¬ WordRepresentable G → ¬ WordRepresentable G.lineGraph := by
  sorry

end LineGraph

modeling_decisions: Graphs are taken to be finite simple graphs: `∀ (V : Type*) [Fintype V] (G : SimpleGraph V)`. Finiteness is essential, not cosmetic: for an infinite edgeless graph, no finite word contains all vertices (so it is non-word-representable) while its line graph is the empty graph (word-representable by the empty word), which would make the statement trivially false.

Word-representability follows Kitaev–Lozin / Kitaev's survey: the word must contain every letter of V at least once; distinct letters x, y alternate iff xy ∈ E. Alternation is formalized as: the word filtered to letters in {x, y} has no two equal consecutive letters (`List.IsChain (· ≠ ·)`), which for x ≠ y is exactly 'of the form xyxy… or yxyx… (even or odd length)'. In particular a permutation of V represents the complete graph, as in the literature.

The `x ≠ y` guard in `Represents` is required: a letter occurring twice never 'alternates with itself', and `G.Adj x x` is false, so dropping the guard would wrongly force every letter to occur at most once.

`[DecidableEq V]` is an instance argument of the definitions (needed for `List.filter`); it does not restrict the class of graphs since every type has a classical `DecidableEq`, and the truth of `WordRepresentable G` does not depend on the instance. It also makes the small `decide`-based API tests possible.

Direction: `answer(True)` means 'yes, the line graph of a non-word-representable graph is always non-word-representable', matching the question. The Wikipedia line-graph article itself does not discuss word-representability; the precise formulation was taken from the Wikipedia list entry and the word-representable-graph literature (Kitaev–Salimov–Severs–Úlfarsson 2011; Kitaev–Lozin 2015; Kitaev's 2017 survey).
The vertex type of `G.lineGraph` is `↥G.edgeSet` (Mathlib's definition); `WordRepresentable` is applied to it with the derived `DecidableEq` on that subtype.
